stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 6.1 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 320 K and 0.97 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 33.0 mL of 0.1 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.15 M NaOH.
5.8 g of $$\ce{KNO3}$$ dissolves in 58 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 11.5 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Mg electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and a Cu electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Cu^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e- -> Mg}$$ E° = -2.37 V; $$\ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e- -> Cu}$$ E° = 0.34 V.
The photoelectron spectra of C (Z = 6) and N (Z = 7) are compared.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 29.8 g. The actual yield is 20 g. What is the percent yield?
What is the pH of a 0.005 M solution of $$\ce{HCl}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] equals its concentration.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0139 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
A reaction has a theoretical yield of 22.8 g. The actual yield is 19.6 g. What is the percent yield?
What is the molecular geometry of $$\ce{NH3}$$?

options.why: Correct. Count electron domains and lone pairs on the central atom.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.

questions.stem: How many formula units or molecules are in 105 g of $$\ce{CH4}$$?

options.why: Correct. Convert grams to moles, then multiply by Avogadro's number.

questions.stem: Which indicator is best for titrating acetic acid with NaOH (equivalence pH ≈ 8.7)?

options.why: Correct. Its range includes the equivalence pH.

questions.explanation: Its range includes the equivalence pH.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{CaO}$$ or $$\ce{MgF2}$$?

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{CaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: $$\ce{MgF2}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{MgF2}$$, because its ions have larger charges

questions.explanation: CaO has ion charges 2 and 2; MgF2 has 2 and 1.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 1.42 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 473 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
A 48.9 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 41.6 mL of 0.207 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 17 L flask at 5.47 atm and 418 K?
At equilibrium, which statement is true?

options.text: Reactant and product concentrations are equal
options.why: They are constant, not necessarily equal.

options.text: Forward and reverse reaction rates are equal

questions.stem: Two buffers have the same pH, but buffer X has ten times the concentration of each component. Which is true?

options.text: Buffer X cannot resist pH changes
Buffer X has a greater buffer capacity
options.why: Correct. More acid and base are available to react.

options.text: Buffer X has a lower pH
options.why: The ratio, and pH, are the same.

questions.explanation: More acid and base are available to react.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 3.6. A mixture has [A] = 0.5 M, [B] = 0.7 M and [C] = 0.1 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.0286
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.0286
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.0286, which is less than K.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.286

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 113 kJ/mol, the transition state at 251 kJ/mol and the products at 119 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 138, ΔH = 6, reverse Ea = 132 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.6 mol N₂, 0.8 mol O₂ and 0.1 mol Ar at a total pressure of 3.5 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of aluminum (Al, Z = 13)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 13 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: 124 g of water at 91 °C is mixed with 157 g of water at 19 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own temperature.
Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.

questions.stem: For the elementary step 2NO + Cl₂ → 2NOCl, what is the rate law?

options.text: It cannot be determined without experiment

options.why: Correct. Elementary steps use their coefficients as exponents.

questions.explanation: Elementary steps use their coefficients as exponents.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.4 mol N₂, 0.1 mol O₂ and 0.6 mol Ar at a total pressure of 3.3 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.04 mol of solute in enough water to make 877 mL of solution?
What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 612 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: A reaction has ΔH° = 90 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 237 J/(mol·K). Above what temperature is it thermodynamically favorable?

options.why: Correct. Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (with ΔH in J).
Convert ΔH to J (or ΔS to kJ).

questions.stem: Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?

options.text: Vaporization separates molecules completely, overcoming all intermolecular forces

questions.stem: 47 mL of 0.6 M solution is diluted to 304 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: How should acetic acid be written in a net ionic equation?

options.text: It is always omitted as a spectator

options.why: Correct. It is a weak acid and mostly un-ionized.

questions.explanation: It is a weak acid and mostly un-ionized.

questions.stem: Which substance has the highest boiling point?

options.why: Correct. Water forms extensive hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: A solid melts at 1,710 °C, is very hard and does not conduct electricity. It is most likely:

options.why: Molecular solids melt at low temperatures.

options.text: An ionic solid that conducts as a solid
options.why: Ionic solids do not conduct as solids.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.8).

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 26. What is K for the reaction multiplied by 2?

options.why: Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.

questions.stem: Why are metals good conductors of electricity?

options.text: Their ions move freely in the solid
options.why: Ions are fixed in the lattice.

options.text: Their valence electrons are delocalized and free to move

questions.stem: Which formula is most likely for the compound of element X (Group 2) and element Y (Group 16)?
Samples of $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{He}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: N2 28, CO2 44, O2 32, He 4.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1 M and [I₂] = 0.8 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.6 M. What is K?
For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, 76 g of $$\ce{N2}$$ reacts with 88 g of $$\ce{H2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{NH3}$$ can form?

options.why: Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Correct. N2 is the limiting reactant.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1 M and [I₂] = 1.2 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.62 M. What is K?
How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{SO4^{2-}}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of a sample of gallium shows two peaks: mass 69 with relative abundance 81% and mass 71 with 19%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.
Pair each mass with its own abundance.
The isotopes are not equally abundant.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.237 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 79 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
98 mL of 8.4 M solution is diluted to 478 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 4.5. In a solution at pH 3.2, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 2.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×2, so order 1 in B.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{BaSO4}$$ is 1.1 \times 10^{-10}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?

options.why: This salt gives two ions: Ksp = s².

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of S in $$\ce{SO4^{2-}}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 101 kJ/mol, the transition state at 248 kJ/mol and the products at 31 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse Ea = transition state − products.
Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 147, ΔH = -70, reverse Ea = 217 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ is consumed at 0.52 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NH3}$$ form?

options.why: Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 2/3.
Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.

questions.stem: Which process has a negative ΔS?
Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -204 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -178 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and reversing reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.
Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.1 M solution of formic acid (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.
Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.5 M solution of hypochlorous acid (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-8})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 2 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 1. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{1}$$, which has 3 electrons.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + Br2 -> 2HBr}$$.

options.why: Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.19 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.2) and 0.45 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.01 mol of HCl is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Correct. First react: H⁺ converts A⁻ to HA. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.

questions.stem: A compound (butane) is 82.7% C, 17.3% H by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to C2H5; the molecular formula is C4H10.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.013 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 62 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature falls by 13.2 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Divide by the moles of reactant.
Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 3420 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -12 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 4.84; K = 127. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: 19 mL of 0.17 M weak acid HA is titrated with 0.3 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH reaches the equivalence point?

options.why: Correct. Moles of base = moles of acid.

questions.stem: What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from these half-cells?

options.why: Cathode minus anode; a galvanic cell is positive.
E° does not change when half-reactions are multiplied.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = 31 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 218 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 964 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Convert ΔS from J to kJ.
Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 1.369 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in ln[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: X → Y + Z. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Mg²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.01 M OH⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Explain how lowering the pH affects the solubility.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: Solubility increases: H⁺ reacts with OH⁻ (a base), shifting the equilibrium toward dissolving.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of N.
Explain why the 1s peak of N has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of C.

rubric.criterion: N has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: N has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: C: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
